newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Opinion polls show Nemtsov most trusted in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Opinion polls show Nemtsov most trusted in Russia.

text.p: Ambitious First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, summoned by President Boris Yeltsin to speed up reforms, has become Russia's most trusted politician, NTV television quoted opinion polls as saying on Sunday.
Nemtsov, whom Yeltsin summoned among other young reformers to whip up stalled reforms, told NTV that he and Yeltsin had smooth relations and compared the president with Russian tsars.

The anchorman of the respected weekly programme Itogi, Yevgeny Kiselyov, said that according to a poll by Public Opinon Foundation in early April among 1,500 Russians, 45 percent of respondents trusted Nemtsov.
Moscow's reformist mayor Yuri Luzhkov, trusted by 37 percent, was the second while nationalist ex-paratroop general Alexander Lebed was third with 35 percent.
It was not clear whether Yeltsin's name was included in either poll list.

Yeltsin, alarmed by widespread public discontent over chronic delays in wages and pensions, dramatically reshuffled his goverment in mid-March to reinforce it with younger, more reform-minded ministers.

He named Nemtsov, 37, governor of Nizhny Novgorod region, and Yeltsin's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, 41, as first deputies to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and gave them a go-ahead to make radical changes aimed at improving the cabinet's performance.
Some analysts speculate that Yeltsin, 66, may have chosen Nemtsov as his unofficial heir and brought the ambitious regional politician to Moscow to train him over the next four years.

In contrast with Chubais, who is a hate figure among Russian conservatives for his role in the bold privatisation campaign, Nemtsov is widely seen as a strong candidate in the next presidential election in the year 2000.
Nemtsov admits that in many ways he is fascinated by once charismatic Yeltsin, who won re-election last summer and cannot run for the third term under the constitution.

"Yeltsin is a real Russian tsar -- reckless, capable of going on a spree, courageous and seldom shy. As opposed to ugly Russian tsars, Yeltsin is a kind tsar," Nemtsov says in his soon-to-be-published book "The Provincial", excerpts from which Kiselyov read out.

Nemtsov marked his arrival in the government with vows to put powerful monopoly structures -- natural gas producer and exporter Gazprom, the national electricity network and railroads -- under stronger government control.
He has been rumoured to have been behind Yeltsin's latest crusade against corruption among government officials, launched by presidential decree last week.
"I have wonderful relations with Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin)," he said smiling. "I have a direct button to contact him him."
